question:
Analise o(s) documento(s) de cenário do projeto e gere o SRS completo no formato especificado, seguindo o processo de trabalho: buscas dedicadas na base de conhecimento para cada tipo de artefato, rastreabilidade validada entre os artefatos.

Documento(s) de cenário:
--- Project Scenario 6.pdf ---
SLCCI (Sea Level Climate Change Initiative)
So here's the deal — this is part of a bigger ESA effort, the Climate Change Initiative,
where they're trying to finally make proper use of thirty-plus years of Earth observation
archives instead of letting all that satellite data just sit there. There are about eleven of
these projects running in parallel, each one looking at a different climate variable, and ours
is the sea level one. Basically the science side has already been doing the heavy lifting —
building the algorithms, validating them, running a kind of prototype production setup —
and now we're at the point where somebody needs to take that prototype and turn it into
something that actually runs operationally, day in day out, and can be handed over to the
people who need the data.
What I picture happening is a system that pulls in altimetry data from a bunch of different
satellite missions, runs it through calibration and validation, cross-calibrates between
missions so everything is consistent, and spits out two kinds of products: one is like a
per-mission track of measurements, and the other is a merged, gridded product that blends
all the missions together into one consistent climate record. On top of that there needs to
be a proper archive, because reprocessing is going to happen again and again as
algorithms improve or new calibration methods come out, so we can't afford to lose the
baseline data or any of the intermediate stuff along the way.
The people using this thing day-to-day are going to be on two very different sides.
Internally you've got the folks who actually run and maintain the production line —
scientists who get pulled in when something needs deeper validation or when a new
product has to be defined, people who just judge and sign off on product quality, people
who handle the catalog and metadata, and then the more operational crowd who monitor
the system, handle incidents, deal with user requests, that sort of thing. Externally, the
audience is really the climate research community — people doing climate modelling work
who just want reliable, well-documented sea level data they can trust and build on. We're
not building this for the general public or commercial customers, it's a fairly specialized
research crowd.
One thing I want to be upfront about: we don't need to worry about near-real-time delivery.
There's a whole separate world of oceanographic services that care about getting data out
within hours for things like operational forecasting, and that's just not us — we're purely
about delayed-time and the long, reprocessed historical series for climate purposes, so
anything geared at that fast-turnaround NRT use case can be dropped from consideration
entirely. Similarly, all that formal IT service management process stuff, incident ticketing
frameworks and so on, isn't something we need to bring in here, it just doesn't fit how this
is going to be run.
Cost is a real concern too, this has to be something that's sustainable to operate long term,
not just a one-off build. And it has to be flexible — new satellite missions are coming online

during the life of the project and the algorithms themselves are going to keep changing as
the science matures, so whatever gets built can't be rigid, it needs to absorb new data
sources and let people swap in improved processing logic without everything falling apart.
There's also a push to not reinvent the wheel — there's existing infrastructure out there
already doing something very similar for ocean data more broadly, and wherever it makes
sense we'd rather lean on what's proven and working than build everything from a blank
page. Quality and traceability of the data matter a lot too, since the whole point is feeding
trustworthy numbers into the international climate change conversation, so whatever
comes out the other end needs solid metadata and documentation attached, not just raw
numbers.

Sistema: SLCCI Operational Sea Level Production System

Resumo executivo: The SLCCI Operational Sea Level Production System transforms the existing scientific prototype into a sustainable operational production environment for processing multi-mission satellite altimetry data. It calibrates, validates, cross-calibrates, archives and publishes traceable along-track and merged gridded sea-level climate products for the climate research community. 

Escopo: Operate a delayed-time production chain that converts multi-mission satellite altimetry observations into validated, documented and traceable sea-level climate records.
  Em escopo: Ingestion of altimetry data from multiple satellite missions
  Em escopo: Calibration, scientific validation and cross-calibration
  Em escopo: Generation of per-mission along-track products
  Em escopo: Generation of merged gridded multi-mission products
  Em escopo: Versioned reprocessing of historical data
  Em escopo: Archival of baseline, intermediate and final datasets
  Em escopo: Metadata, provenance and documentation management
  Em escopo: Product quality review and approval
  Em escopo: Cataloguing, search and distribution to climate researchers
  Em escopo: Operational monitoring and failure notification
  Em escopo: Configurable onboarding of new satellite missions and algorithms
  Em escopo: Reuse and integration of suitable existing ocean-data infrastructure
  Fora de escopo: Near-real-time data delivery — the project addresses delayed-time climate records
  Fora de escopo: Operational ocean forecasting — addressed by separate oceanographic services
  Fora de escopo: General-public or commercial data services — the target audience is the climate research community
  Fora de escopo: Formal IT service-management and incident-ticketing frameworks — explicitly excluded from the operating model
  Fora de escopo: Development of satellite instruments or acquisition systems — the system consumes existing mission data
  Premissa: PA-01: Satellite missions or their data providers make source altimetry datasets available in documented formats.
  Premissa: PA-02: Scientific teams provide validated calibration, validation and merging algorithms.
  Premissa: PA-03: Product quality assessors have authority to approve or reject product releases.
  Premissa: PA-04: [INFERRED] Existing ocean-data infrastructure exposes interfaces suitable for evaluation and integration.
  Premissa: PA-05: [INFERRED] Climate researchers can access published products through network-based catalog and download services.
  Restrição: REST-01 (Operational): Products shall be generated exclusively in delayed-time mode.
  Restrição: REST-02 (Financial): Long-term operational and storage costs must remain sustainable.
  Restrição: REST-03 (Technical): New missions and algorithm versions must be incorporated without redesigning the complete production chain.
  Restrição: REST-04 (Architectural): Proven existing infrastructure should be reused where technically and economically suitable.
  Restrição: REST-05 (Data governance): Baseline, intermediate and final data must remain traceable across repeated reprocessing cycles.
  Restrição: REST-06 (Service management): Formal ITSM and incident-ticketing frameworks shall not be required.

Stakeholders:
  STK-01 - ESA Climate Change Initiative programme (Stakeholder externo): Sustainable operational production, trustworthy climate records and alignment with the broader Climate Change Initiative.
  STK-02 - Production operator (Usuário primário): Configure, execute, monitor and recover delayed-time processing and reprocessing runs.
  STK-03 - Sea-level scientist (Usuário primário): Configure scientific algorithms, perform deeper validation and define new climate products.
  STK-04 - Product quality assessor (Usuário secundário): Review validation evidence and approve or reject products before publication.
  STK-05 - Catalog and metadata manager (Usuário secundário): Maintain complete metadata, provenance, documentation and catalog records.
  STK-06 - Operations support staff (Usuário primário): Monitor service health, diagnose failures and respond to operational or user issues without formal ITSM tooling.
  STK-07 - Climate researcher and climate modeller (Stakeholder externo): Discover and retrieve reliable, consistent and documented historical sea-level datasets.
  STK-08 - Satellite mission data provider (Stakeholder externo): Provide source altimetry data and associated mission documentation through stable interfaces.
  STK-09 - Existing ocean-data infrastructure provider (Stakeholder externo): Provide reusable infrastructure capabilities and documented integration interfaces.

Regras de negócio:
  RN-001 - Delayed-time production: Sea-level climate products are produced from delayed-time observations and historical reprocessing rather than near-real-time data streams.
  RN-002 - Multi-mission consistency: Measurements originating from different satellite missions must be cross-calibrated before they are combined into a common climate record.
  RN-003 - Required product families: Production must provide both per-mission along-track measurement products and merged gridded multi-mission products.
  RN-004 - Preservation of processing stages: Baseline observations, required intermediate datasets and final products must be preserved to support future reprocessing and scientific audit.
  RN-005 - Versioned reprocessing: Each reprocessing cycle must be identified by the source-data baseline, algorithm versions, calibration configuration and product version.
  RN-006 - Quality approval before publication: A product version may be released to external researchers only after its quality evidence has been reviewed and approved.
  RN-007 - Mandatory product documentation: Every published product must include metadata, provenance, quality information and documentation sufficient to interpret and reproduce its processing history.
  RN-008 - Specialised research distribution: Published products are intended for climate research and climate-modelling use rather than general-public, commercial or operational forecasting services.
  RN-009 - Reuse of proven capabilities: Existing infrastructure capabilities should be reused when they satisfy scientific, operational, financial and traceability needs.

Requisitos funcionais:
  RF-001 - Ingest mission data: The system shall ingest altimetry datasets from each configured satellite mission. [Must have]
  RF-002 - Validate ingested data: The system shall validate each ingested dataset against its configured format, mandatory fields and integrity checks. [Must have]
  RF-003 - Calibrate mission observations: The system shall apply the selected calibration configuration to each accepted mission dataset. [Must have]

  RF-005 - Cross-calibrate missions: The system shall apply the selected cross-calibration method to observations from different missions. [Must have]
  RF-006 - Generate along-track products: The system shall generate a versioned along-track sea-level product for each processed mission. [Must have]
  RF-007 - Generate merged gridded products: The system shall generate a versioned gridded sea-level product by merging eligible cross-calibrated mission observations. [Must have]
  RF-008 - Manage algorithm versions: The system shall register each processing algorithm with a unique version and applicable configuration. [Must have]
  RF-009 - Execute historical reprocessing: The system shall execute a reprocessing run for a selected historical period, mission set, data baseline and algorithm version. [Must have]
  RF-010 - Archive baseline data: The system shall archive every accepted baseline dataset with its checksum and source identifier. [Must have]
  RF-011 - Archive intermediate data: The system shall archive each intermediate dataset designated as required by the active retention policy. [Must have]
  RF-012 - Archive final products: The system shall archive every generated final product as an immutable versioned object. [Must have]
  RF-013 - Record processing provenance: The system shall record the source datasets, algorithms, configurations, execution time and processing steps used for each product. [Must have]
  RF-014 - Manage product metadata: The system shall associate each final product with its mandatory scientific, temporal, spatial, quality and provenance metadata. [Must have]
  RF-015 - Approve product releases: The system shall permit an authorised quality assessor to approve or reject a product version with a recorded justification. [Must have]
  RF-016 - Catalogue published products: The system shall add each approved product version and its documentation to the searchable product catalogue. [Must have]
  RF-017 - Provide product retrieval: The system shall allow climate researchers to retrieve an approved product and its associated documentation. [Must have]
  RF-018 - Monitor production runs: The system shall display the current state and execution history of each production or reprocessing run. [Must have]
  RF-019 - Notify processing failures: The system shall notify configured operations personnel when a processing run enters a failed state. [Should have]
  RF-020 - Configure new missions: The system shall allow an authorised operator to register a new satellite mission through a configurable mission definition. [Must have]
  RF-021 - Integrate reusable infrastructure: The system shall exchange datasets and metadata with each approved existing infrastructure service through a documented interface. [Should have]

Glossário:
  Altimetry: Measurement of sea-surface height using satellite-based radar observations.
  Along-track product: A sea-level dataset retaining measurements along the observation track of an individual satellite mission.
  Baseline data: Accepted source observations used as the starting point for one or more processing or reprocessing cycles.
  Calibration: Application of corrections and reference adjustments to mission observations.
  Cross-calibration: Adjustment and comparison of observations from different missions to produce a consistent multi-mission record.
  Delayed-time: Processing performed after observations and required auxiliary information are available, without near-real-time delivery constraints.
  Gridded product: A dataset in which merged observations are represented on a defined spatial and temporal grid.
  NRT: Near-real-time processing intended to deliver observations shortly after acquisition; excluded from this system.
  Product version: Immutable identification of a product generated from a specific baseline, algorithm set and processing configuration.
  Provenance: Recorded lineage connecting a product to its source datasets, algorithms, configurations and processing events.
  Reprocessing: Regeneration of historical products using revised algorithms, calibration methods, configurations or input baselines.
  SLCCI: Sea Level Climate Change Initiative, the sea-level component of ESA's Climate Change Initiative.

Propósito

Propósito

SLCCI (Sea Level Climate Change Initiative)
So here's the deal — this is part of a bigger ESA effort, the Climate Change Initiative,
where they're trying to finally make proper use of thirty-plus years of Earth observation
archives instead of letting all that satellite data just sit there. There are about eleven of
these projects running in parallel, each one looking at a different climate variable, and ours
is the sea level one. Basically the science side has already been doing the heavy lifting —
building the algorithms, validating them, running a kind of prototype production setup —
and now we're at the point where somebody needs to take that prototype and turn it into
something that actually runs operationally, day in day out, and can be handed over to the
people who need the data.
What I picture happening is a system that pulls in altimetry data from a bunch of different
satellite missions, runs it through calibration and validation, cross-calibrates between
missions so everything is consistent, and spits out two kinds of products: one is like a
per-mission track of measurements, and the other is a merged, gridded product that blends
all the missions together into one consistent climate record. On top of that there needs to
be a proper archive, because reprocessing is going to happen again and again as
algorithms improve or new calibration methods come out, so we can't afford to lose the
baseline data or any of the intermediate stuff along the way.
The people using this thing day-to-day are going to be on two very different sides.
Internally you've got the folks who actually run and maintain the production line —
scientists who get pulled in when something needs deeper validation or when a new
product has to be defined, people who just judge and sign off on product quality, people
who handle the catalog and metadata, and then the more operational crowd who monitor
the system, handle incidents, deal with user requests, that sort of thing. Externally, the
audience is really the climate research community — people doing climate modelling work
who just want reliable, well-documented sea level data they can trust and build on. We're
not building this for the general public or commercial customers, it's a fairly specialized
research crowd.
One thing I want to be upfront about: we don't need to worry about near-real-time delivery.
There's a whole separate world of oceanographic services that care about getting data out
within hours for things like operational forecasting, and that's just not us — we're purely
about delayed-time and the long, reprocessed historical series for climate purposes, so
anything geared at that fast-turnaround NRT use case can be dropped from consideration
entirely. Similarly, all that formal IT service management process stuff, incident ticketing

Expected challenges
The presence of an existing system leads to common challenges that both enhancement and 
replacement projects will face, including the following:
■ The changes made could degrade the performance to which users are accustomed.
■ Little or no requirements documentation might be available for the existing system.
■ Users who are familiar with how the system works today might not like the changes they are 
about to encounter.
■ You might unknowingly break or omit functionality that is vital to some stakeholder group.
■ Stakeholders might take this opportunity to request new functionality that seems like a good 
idea but isn’t really needed to meet the business objectives.
Even if there is existing documentation, it might not prove useful. For enhancement projects, 
the documentation might not be up to date. If the documentation doesn’t match the existing 
application’s reality, it is of limited use. For replacement systems, you also need to be wary of carrying 
forward all of the requirements, because some of the old functionality probably should not be 
migrated.
One of the major issues in replacement projects is validating that the reasons for the replacement 
are sound. There need to be justifiable business objectives for the change. When existing systems 
are being completely replaced, organizational processes might also have to change, which makes it 
harder for people to accept a new system. The change in business processes, change in the software 
system, and learning curve of a new system can disrupt current operations.

O Documento de Especificação de Requisitos de Software (SRS) é o contrato técnico que descreve o

1.1 Artefatos Obrigatórios e sua Ordem
Um SRS completo e formal deve conter os seguintes artefatos, nesta ordem:
• ESCOPO: Define o que está DENTRO e FORA do projeto. Evita scope creep.
• STAKEHOLDERS: Lista todos os envolvidos: quem usa, quem financia, quem é afetado.
• PREMISSAS E RESTRIÇÕES: Fatos assumidos como verdadeiros e limites impostos ao projeto.
• REGRAS DE NEGÓCIO (RN): Políticas, fórmulas e condições de negócio que existem independentemente 
do software.
• REQUISITOS FUNCIONAIS (RF): O que o sistema DEVE FAZER — comportamentos, serviços, respostas a 
entradas.
• REQUISITOS NÃO FUNCIONAIS (RNF): Como o sistema deve SER — atributos de qualidade 
quantificáveis.
• HISTÓRIAS DE USUÁRIO (HU): Necessidades na perspectiva do usuário: Como [perfil], quero [ação], para
[benefício].
• CASOS DE USO (UC): Interações detalhadas ator-sistema com fluxo principal, alternativo e exceções.
• CRITÉRIOS DE ACEITE (CA): Condições testáveis em formato BDD (Dado/Quando/Então) que definem

• GLOSSÁRIO: Termos do domínio com definição precisa para eliminar ambiguidades.

Which requirements should you specify?
It’s not always worth taking the time to generate a complete set of requirements for an entire 
production system. Many options lie between the two extremes of continuing forever with no 
requirements documentation and reconstructing a perfect requirements set. Knowing why you’d like 
to have written requirements available lets you judge whether the cost of rebuilding all—or even 
part—of the specification is a sound investment.

Rarely do you need to document the entire existing system. Focus detailed requirements efforts 
on the changes needed to meet the business objectives. If you’re replacing a system, start by 
documenting the areas prioritized as most important to achieve the business objectives or those that 
pose the highest implementation risk. Any new requirements identified during the gap analysis will 
need to be specified at the same level of precision and using the same techniques as you would for a 
new system.
Level of detail
One of the biggest challenges is determining the appropriate level of detail at which to document 
requirements gleaned from the existing system. For enhancements, defining requirements for the 
new functionality alone might be sufficient. However, you will usually benefit from documenting all of 
the functionality that closely relates to the enhancement, to ensure that the change fits in seamlessly 
(region B in Figure 21-2). You might want to create business processes, user requirements, and/or 
functional requirements for those related areas. For example, let’s say you are adding a discount code 
feature to an existing shopping cart function, but you don’t have any documented requirements for 
the shopping cart. You might be tempted to write just a single user story: “As a customer, I need to be 
able to enter a discount code so I can get the cheapest price for the product.” However, this user story 
alone lacks context, so consider capturing other user stories about shopping cart operations. That 
information could be valuable the next time you need to modify the shopping cart function.
I worked with one team that was just beginning to develop the requirements for version 2 of 
a major product with embedded software. They hadn’t done a good job on the requirements for 
version 1, which was currently being implemented. The lead BA wondered, “Is it worth going back 
to improve the SRS for version 1?” The company anticipated that this product line would be a major 
revenue generator for at least 10 years. They also planned to reuse some of the core requirements 
in several spin-off products. In this case, it made sense to improve the requirements documentation 
for version 1 because it was the foundation for all subsequent development work in this product line.

CHAPTER 6 Finding the voice of the user 107
Consider building a catalog of user classes that recur across multiple applications. Defining user 
classes at the enterprise level lets you reuse those user class descriptions in future projects. The next 
system you build might serve the needs of some new user classes, but it probably will also be used 
by user classes from your earlier systems. If you do include the user-class descriptions in the project’s 
SRS, you can incorporate entries from the reusable user-class catalog by reference and just write 
descriptions of any new groups that are specific to that application.
User personas
To help bring your user classes to life, consider creating a persona for each one, a description of a 
representative member of the user class (Cooper 2004; Leffingwell 2011). A persona is a description 
of a hypothetical, generic person who serves as a stand-in for a group of users having similar 
characteristics and needs. You can use personas to help you understand the requirements and to 
design the user experience to best meet the needs of specific user communities.
A persona can serve as a placeholder when the BA doesn’t have an actual user representative 
at hand. Rather than having progress come to a halt, the BA can envision a persona performing 
a particular task or try to assess what the persona’s preferences would be, thereby drafting a 
requirements starting point to be confirmed when an actual user is available. Persona details for a 
commercial customer include social and demographic characteristics and behaviors, preferences, 
annoyances, and similar information. Make sure the personas you create truly are representative of 
their user class, based on market, demographic, and ethnographic research.
Here’s an example of a persona for one user class on the Chemical Tracking System:
Fred, 41, has been a chemist at Contoso Pharmaceuticals since he received his Ph.D. 
14 years ago. He doesn’t have much patience with computers. Fred usually works 
on two projects at a time in related chemical areas. His lab contains approximately 
300 bottles of chemicals and gas cylinders. On an average day, he’ll need four new 
chemicals from the stockroom. Two of these will be commercial chemicals in stock, 
one will need to be ordered, and one will come from the supply of proprietary Contoso 
chemical samples. On occasion, Fred will need a hazardous chemical that requires 
special training for safe handling. When he buys a chemical for the first time, Fred 
wants the material safety data sheet emailed to him automatically. Each year, Fred will 
synthesize about 20 new proprietary chemicals to go into the stockroom. Fred wants 
a report of his chemical usage for the previous month to be generated automatically 
and sent to him by email so that he can monitor his chemical exposure.
As the business analyst explores the chemists’ requirements, he can think about Fred as the archetype 
of this user class and ask himself, “What would Fred need to do?” Working with a persona makes the 
requirements thought process more tangible than if you simply contemplate what a whole faceless 
group of people might want. Some people choose a random human face of the appropriate gender 
to make a persona seem even more real.108 PART II Requirements development
Dean Leffingwell (2011) suggests that you design the system to make it easy for the individual 
described in your persona to use the application. That is, you focus on meeting that one (imaginary) 
person’s needs. Provided you’ve created a persona that accurately represents the user class, this 
should help you do a good job of satisfying the needs and expectations of the whole class.

Examine existing system interfaces to determine what 
data is exchanged between systems today. Understand how users use the current system. If no one 
understands the functionality and business rules behind the user interface, someone will need to look 
at the code or database to understand what’s going on. Analyze any documentation that does 
exist—design documents, help screens, user manuals, training materials—to identify requirements.
You might not need to specify functional requirements for the existing system at all, instead 
creating models to fill the information void. Swimlane diagrams can describe how users do their jobs 
with the system today. Context diagrams, data flow diagrams, and entity-relationship diagrams are 
also useful. You might create user requirements, specifying them only at a high level without filling 
in all of the details. Another way to begin closing the information gap is to create data dictionary 
entries when you add new data elements to the system and modify existing definitions. The test suite 
might be useful as an initial source of information to recover the software requirements, because tests 
represent an alternative view of requirements.CHAPTER 21 Enhancement and replacement projects 401
Sometimes “good enough” is enough
A third-party assessment of current business analysis practices in one organization revealed 
that their teams did a fairly good job of writing requirements for new projects, but they failed 
to update the requirements as the products evolved through a series of enhancement releases. 
The BAs did create requirements for each enhancement project. However, they did not merge 
all of those revisions back into the requirements baseline. The organization’s manager couldn’t 
think of a measurable benefit from keeping the existing documentation 100 percent updated 
to reflect the implemented systems. He assumed that his requirements always reflected only 
80 to 90 percent of the working software anyway, so there was little value in trying to perfect 
the requirements for an enhancement. This meant that future enhancement project teams 
would have to work with some uncertainty and close the gaps when needed, but that price was 
deemed acceptable.
Encouraging new system adoption
You’re bound to run into resistance when changing or replacing an existing system. People are 
naturally reluctant to change. Introducing a new feature that will make users’ jobs easier is a good 
thing. But users are accustomed to how the system works today, and you plan to modify that, which 
is not so good from the user’s point of view. The issue is even bigger when you’re replacing a system, 
because now you’re changing more than just a bit of functionality. You’re potentially changing the 
entire application’s look and feel, its menus, the operating environment, and possibly the user’s 
whole job. If you're a business analyst, project manager, or project sponsor, you have to anticipate the 
resistance and plan how you will overcome it, so the users will accept the new features or system.
An existing, established system is probably stable, fully integrated with surrounding systems, and 
well understood by users. A new system with all the same functionality might be none of these upon 
its initial release. Users might fear that the new system will disrupt their normal operations while 
they learn how to use it. Even worse, it might not support their current operations. Users might even 
be afraid of losing their jobs if the system automates tasks they perform manually today. It’s not 
uncommon to hear users say that they will accept the new system only if it does everything the old 
system does—even if they don’t personally use all of that functionality at present.
To mitigate the risk of user resistance, you first need to understand the business objectives and 
the user requirements. If either of these misses the mark, you will lose the users’ trust quickly.

Locking a user’s account after four unsuccessful login attempts protects against access by the 
disfavored user class of “user impersonators,” albeit at the risk of inconveniencing forgetful legitimate 
users. If my bank doesn’t recognize the computer I’m using, it sends me an email message with a 
one-time access code I have to enter before I can log on. This feature was implemented because of 
the disfavored user class of “people who might have stolen my banking information.”
You might elect to ignore still other user classes. Yes, they will use the product, but you don’t 
specifically build it to suit them. If there are any other groups of users that are neither favored, 
disfavored, nor ignored, they are of equal importance in defining the product’s requirements.
Each user class will have its own set of requirements for the tasks that members of the class must 
perform. There could be some overlap between the needs of different user classes. Tellers, business 
bankers, and loan officers all might have to check a bank customer’s account balance, for instance. 
Different user classes also could have different quality expectations, such as usability, that will drive 
user interface design choices. New or occasional users are concerned with how easy the system is to 
learn. Such users like menus, graphical user interfaces, uncluttered screen displays, wizards, and help 
screens. As users gain experience with the system, they become more interested in efficiency. They 
now value keyboard shortcuts, customization options, toolbars, and scripting facilities.
Trap Don’t overlook indirect user classes. They won’t use your application themselves, 
instead accessing its data or services through other applications or through reports. Your 
customer once removed is still your customer.
User classes need not be human beings. They could be software agents performing a service on 
behalf of a human user, such as bots. Software agents can scan networks for information about goods 
and services, assemble custom news feeds, process your incoming email, monitor physical systems 
and networks for problems or intrusions, or perform data mining. Internet agents that probe websites 
for vulnerabilities or to generate spam are a type of disfavored non-human user class. If you identify 
these sorts of disfavored user classes, you might specify certain requirements not to meet their needs 
but rather to thwart them. For instance, website tools such as CAPTCHA that validate whether a user is 
a human being attempt to block such disruptive access by “users” you want to keep out.
Remember, users are a subset of customers, which are a subset of stakeholders. You’ll need to 
consider a much broader range of potential sources of requirements than just direct and indirect user 
classes. For instance, even though the development team members aren’t end users of the system 
they’re building, you need their input on internal quality attributes such as efficiency, modifiability, 
portability, and reusability, as described in Chapter 14, “Beyond functionality.” One company 
found that every installation of their product was an expensive nightmare until they introduced an 
“installer” user class so they could focus on requirements such as the development of a customization 
architecture for their product. Look well beyond the obvious end users when you’re trying to identify 
stakeholders whose requirements input is necessary.

in the current system. Even the existing functionality has to map to current and anticipated business 
objectives to warrant re-implementing it in the new system.
Trap Don’t let stakeholders get away with saying “I have it today, so I need it in the new 
system” as a default method of justifying requirements.
Mind the gap
A gap analysis is a comparison of functionality between an existing system and a desired new system. 
A gap analysis can be expressed in different ways, including use cases, user stories, or features. When 
enhancing an existing system, perform a gap analysis to make sure you understand why it isn’t 
currently meeting your business objectives.
Gap analysis for a replacement project entails understanding existing functionality and discovering 
the desired new functionality (see Figure 21-1). Identify user requirements for the existing system that 
stakeholders want to have re-implemented in the new system. Also, elicit new user requirements that 
the existing system does not address. Consider any change requests that were never implemented CHAPTER 21 Enhancement and replacement projects 397
in the existing system. Prioritize the existing user requirements and the new ones together. Prioritize 
closing the gaps using business objectives as described in the previous section or the other 
prioritization techniques presented in Chapter 16, “First things first: Setting requirement priorities.”
FIGURE 21-1 When you are replacing an existing system, some requirements will be implemented unchanged, 
some will be modified, some will be discarded, and some new requirements might be added.
Maintaining performance levels
Existing systems set user expectations for performance and throughput. Stakeholders almost 
always have key performance indicators (KPIs) for existing processes that they will want to maintain 
in the new system. A key performance indicator model (KPIM) can help you identify and specify 
these metrics for their corresponding business processes (Beatty and Chen 2012). The KPIM helps 
stakeholders see that even if the new system will be different, their business outcomes will be at least 
as good as before.
Unless you explicitly plan to maintain them, performance levels can be compromised as systems 
are enhanced. Stuffing new functionality into an existing system might slow it down. One data 
synchronization tool had a requirement to update a master data set from the day’s transactions. 
It needed to run every 24 hours. In the initial release of the tool, the synchronization started at 
midnight and took about one hour to execute. After some enhancements to include additional 
attributes, merging, and synchronicity checks, the synchronization took 20 hours to execute. This was 
a problem, because users expected to have fully synchronized data from the night before available 
when they started their workday at 8:00 A.M. The maximum time to complete the synchronization 
was never explicitly specified, but the stakeholders assumed it could be done overnight in less than 
eight hours.
For replacement systems, prioritize the KPIs that are most important to maintain. Look for the 
business processes that trace to the most important KPIs and the requirements that enable those 
business processes; these are the requirements to implement first. For instance, if you’re replacing a 
loan application system in which loan processors can enter 10 loans per day, it might be important 
to maintain at least that same throughput in the new system. The functionality that allows loan 
processers to enter loans should be some of the earliest implemented in the new system, so the loan 
processors can maintain their productivity.

6. Security (Segurança)
 Confidentiality — dados acessíveis apenas por autorizados.
 Integrity — dados protegidos contra alteração não autorizada.
 Non-repudiation — ações não podem ser negadas.
 Accountability — ações rastreáveis ao usuário.
 Authenticity — identidade verificável.
 Resistance — proteção contra ataques.

7. Maintainability (Manutenibilidade)
 Modularity — componentes independentes com impacto isolado de mudanças.
 Reusability — componentes reutilizáveis em outros contextos.
 Analysability — facilidade de diagnóstico de falhas.

Externally, the
audience is really the climate research community — people doing climate modelling work
who just want reliable, well-documented sea level data they can trust and build on. We're
not building this for the general public or commercial customers, it's a fairly specialized
research crowd.
One thing I want to be upfront about: we don't need to worry about near-real-time delivery.
There's a whole separate world of oceanographic services that care about getting data out
within hours for things like operational forecasting, and that's just not us — we're purely
about delayed-time and the long, reprocessed historical series for climate purposes, so
anything geared at that fast-turnaround NRT use case can be dropped from consideration
entirely. Similarly, all that formal IT service management process stuff, incident ticketing
frameworks and so on, isn't something we need to bring in here, it just doesn't fit how this
is going to be run.
Cost is a real concern too, this has to be something that's sustainable to operate long term,
not just a one-off build. And it has to be flexible — new satellite missions are coming onlineduring the life of the project and the algorithms themselves are going to keep changing as
the science matures, so whatever gets built can't be rigid, it needs to absorb new data
sources and let people swap in improved processing logic without everything falling apart.
There's also a push to not reinvent the wheel — there's existing infrastructure out there
already doing something very similar for ocean data more broadly, and wherever it makes
sense we'd rather lean on what's proven and working than build everything from a blank
page. Quality and traceability of the data matter a lot too, since the whole point is feeding
trustworthy numbers into the international climate change conversation, so whatever
comes out the other end needs solid metadata and documentation attached, not just raw
numbers.

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The mission and its input format are configured.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The validated dataset is registered and archived as an accepted baseline.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: The dataset remains rejected and no processing task is started.
fluxo_principal: 1. The operator selects a mission dataset for ingestion.
2. The system reads the mission configuration.
3. The system validates the format, mandatory fields and checksum.
4. The system registers and archives the accepted baseline dataset.
5. The system reports successful ingestion.
fluxos_alternativos: 3a. A nonmandatory field is absent → the system records a warning and continues validation.
fluxos_excecao: 3b. A mandatory field or checksum is invalid → the system rejects the dataset and records the validation errors (ref. RN-004, RF-002).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: An accepted baseline dataset and approved calibration configuration exist.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: Calibrated observations and scientific validation evidence are stored.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: No output is released and the failure evidence is retained.
fluxo_principal: 1. The scientist selects the dataset and calibration configuration.
2. The system applies the calibration algorithm.
3. The system executes the scientific validation checks.
4. The system stores the calibrated observations and validation evidence.
fluxos_alternativos: 3a. A validation warning threshold is reached → the system marks the output for scientific review.
fluxos_excecao: 2b. Calibration execution fails → the system marks the run as failed and preserves diagnostic information (ref. RF-003).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: Eligible calibrated observations from the selected missions are available.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: A versioned merged gridded product is generated with provenance.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: No merged product version is created.
fluxo_principal: 1. The scientist selects missions, temporal coverage and product configuration.
2. The system cross-calibrates the selected observations.
3. The system merges the eligible observations onto the configured grid.
4. The system generates a versioned product.
5. The system records the product provenance.
fluxos_alternativos: 2a. A mission is outside the selected temporal coverage → the system excludes that mission and continues.
fluxos_excecao: 2b. Cross-calibration fails its configured checks → the system stops generation and records the failure (ref. RN-002, RF-005).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The selected baseline data, algorithms and configurations are available.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: A traceable new product version is generated for the requested historical period.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: Previous product versions remain unchanged and available.
fluxo_principal: 1. The operator selects the historical period and missions.
2. The operator selects the baseline and algorithm versions.
3. The system validates that all required inputs are available.
4. The system executes the reprocessing chain.
5. The system archives the outputs and provenance.
fluxos_alternativos: 3a. Optional intermediate data is absent → the system reproduces it from the archived baseline.
fluxos_excecao: 3b. A required baseline object is unavailable → the system prevents execution and identifies the missing object (ref. RN-004, RF-009).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The product and its validation evidence are complete and pending review.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The product is approved and becomes eligible for publication.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: The product remains unavailable to external researchers.
fluxo_principal: 1. The assessor opens the pending product version.
2. The system presents validation evidence, metadata and provenance.
3. The assessor records an approval justification.
4. The system records the decision and marks the product as approved.
fluxos_alternativos: 3a. The assessor rejects the product → the system records the justification and marks the product as rejected.
fluxos_excecao: 2b. Mandatory evidence is missing → the system prevents approval and lists the missing information (ref. RN-006, RF-015).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The product is approved and has mandatory metadata and documentation.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The product is searchable and available to authorised researchers.
fluxo_principal: 1. The manager selects an approved product.
2. The system validates metadata and documentation completeness.
3. The manager confirms publication.
4. The system creates the catalogue entry.
5. The system marks the product as published.
fluxos_alternativos: 2a. Optional metadata is absent → the system displays a warning and permits publication.
fluxos_excecao: 2b. Mandatory metadata is absent → the system blocks publication and lists the missing fields (ref. RN-007, RF-014).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: At least one approved product is published.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The researcher obtains the selected product and documentation.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: No incomplete or unapproved product is delivered.
fluxo_principal: 1. The researcher searches by product type, mission, period or version.
2. The system returns matching published products.
3. The researcher selects a product.
4. The system presents metadata and documentation.
5. The researcher requests retrieval.
6. The system provides the product and verifies its checksum.
fluxos_alternativos: 2a. No product matches → the system returns an empty result with the applied filters.
fluxos_excecao: 6b. Integrity verification fails → the system prevents delivery and records the affected object (ref. RF-017, RNF-006).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: A production or reprocessing run exists.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The operator obtains the current state and execution history.
fluxo_principal: 1. The operator opens the run-monitoring view.
2. The system lists active and completed runs.
3. The operator selects a run.
4. The system displays its state, progress, timestamps and processing history.
fluxos_alternativos: 2a. The operator applies mission, state or date filters → the system updates the list.
fluxos_excecao: 3b. The run identifier no longer exists → the system reports that the run was not found (ref. RF-018).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: The operator is authorised and mission interface documentation is available.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: The mission is available for test ingestion and processing.
fluxo_principal: 1. The operator creates a mission definition.
2. The operator specifies source interfaces, formats and validation rules.
3. The operator associates calibration and processing configurations.
4. The system validates the definition using reference data.
5. The operator activates the mission.
fluxos_alternativos: 4a. Validation produces nonblocking warnings → the operator records a justification and continues.
fluxos_excecao: 4b. Mandatory validation fails → the system prevents activation and reports the failed rules (ref. RF-020).

casos_de_uso.pre_condicao: An infrastructure service has been approved for reuse.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_sucesso: Datasets and metadata can be exchanged through the configured interface.
casos_de_uso.pos_condicao_falha: The integration remains inactive and production is not redirected to it.
fluxo_principal: 1. The operator registers the external service endpoint.
2. The system validates connectivity and authentication.

stakeholders.descricao: Scientists — brought in for deeper validation or definition of new products.
Quality reviewers — evaluate and sign off on generated products before release.
Catalog/metadata staff — maintain the product catalog and metadata.
Operational staff — monitor the system, handle incidents, and respond to user requests.
Climate research community (external users) — researchers doing climate modelling who need reliable, well-documented sea level data.

regras_de_negocio.descricao: The system is one of about eleven parallel ESA Climate Change Initiative projects, each covering a different climate variable — this project covers sea level.
Products must go through calibration, validation, and cross-calibration between missions before being considered consistent.
Reprocessing happens repeatedly as algorithms and calibration methods evolve, so baseline and intermediate data must never be lost.
The target audience is exclusively the climate research community — not the general public or commercial customers.
Near-real-time (NRT) delivery use cases are explicitly excluded — the system only serves the reprocessed/delayed-time data flow.

historias_de_usuario.descricao: As a scientist, I want to perform deeper validation or define new products when needed, so that scientific quality is maintained as the system evolves.
As a quality reviewer, I want to evaluate and approve products, so that only validated data is released.
As a member of the catalog/metadata team, I want to maintain the product catalog and metadata, so that the data stays discoverable and well-documented.
As a member of the operational staff, I want to monitor the system, handle incidents, and respond to user requests, so that day-to-day operations keep running.
As a climate research community member, I want to access reliable, well-documented sea level data, so that I can trust it and build my research on it.

As a system operator, I want to reprocess historical data when algorithms or calibration methods improve, without losing baseline or intermediate data, so that the climate record stays accurate over time.

casos_de_uso.descricao: Process satellite altimetry data — the system ingests data from multiple missions, calibrates and validates it, cross-calibrates between missions, and generates the per-mission and multi-mission gridded products.
Review and release product — a quality reviewer evaluates a newly generated product and approves it for release, or flags it for correction.
Reprocess historical data — an operator triggers reprocessing of archived baseline/intermediate data using an updated algorithm or calibration method, without losing prior data.
Onboard new satellite mission — an operator or scientist configures the system to ingest data from a newly available satellite mission.

criterios_de_aceite.descricao: Given altimetry data from two or more satellite missions, when cross-calibration is performed, then the resulting measurements are consistent across missions.
Given a reprocessing run using an updated algorithm, when processing completes, then the baseline and intermediate data from previous runs remain intact and accessible.
Given a newly generated product, when a quality reviewer evaluates it, then the product is approved for release or flagged for correction.
Given a released dataset, when a climate research community member accesses it, then the dataset includes metadata and documentation sufficient to trace its origin and processing history.
Given a new satellite mission becomes available, when it is onboarded, then that mission's data is processed without requiring a rebuild of the existing processing pipelines.
